title: Blunt Abdominal Trauma - 16-Year-Old after a Bicycle Fall with LUQ Pain
patient_instructions: You are Jayden Marsh, 16 years old, brought to the Emergency Department after falling off your bike about an hour ago. You swerved to avoid a car and came off, landing on your left side and hitting the handlebars into your left upper tummy. You have constant, worsening pain in the left upper part of your stomach. If asked specifically: you feel a bit dizzy; you did not clearly lose consciousness but things were a blur for a moment; you did not hit your head; you feel slightly sick but have not vomited blood; no blood in stool; you have not passed urine since the fall so you are unsure about blood in the urine; mild pain at the top of your left shoulder if the candidate asks about shoulder-tip pain. No shortness of breath, no chest pain, no palpitations at rest. No past medical history, no regular medications, no blood thinners. Ideas: you think you have 'just winded yourself'. Concerns: you are scared and want your mum. Expectations: you want the pain to stop and to know you are okay. Affect: frightened teenager, a little breathless from anxiety, cooperative. Use everyday language.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor in a rural NSW Emergency Department. Jayden Marsh, a 16-year-old boy, has arrived after a bicycle fall with left upper quadrant pain. Tasks: (1) Confirm haemodynamic stability, then take a focused trauma history for approximately 5 minutes, screening the organs and systems at risk. (2) Explain your working diagnosis and differentials to the patient. (3) Outline your immediate management and investigations in the ED. Manage as per an Australian ED with retrieval available to a tertiary centre.
examiner_instructions: This is a time-critical trauma station. Reward candidates who frame the approach with primary survey / EMST principles, confirm haemodynamic stability, and run a structured injury screen of the high-risk LUQ organs (spleen, kidney) plus GI, respiratory and cardiovascular systems, screening for head injury and loss of consciousness first. Kehr's sign (left shoulder-tip pain) is a high-yield splenic-injury question. Expected differentials: splenic and renal injury, rib fracture/lung contusion, bowel injury, cardiac tamponade. Management should be investigation-led: eFAST, CXR, FBE, group and cross-match, urinalysis, analgesia, IV access, admission and close monitoring. Reward candidates who state that haemodynamically STABLE splenic/renal injuries are managed non-operatively (observation +/- embolisation), with laparotomy reserved for instability. Prompt if needed: 'How does his stability change your plan?'

criteria: Confirms haemodynamic stability and frames approach with primary survey / EMST
Explores the mechanism (direct blow, handlebars, side landing) and screens for head injury and loss of consciousness
Structured injury screen of spleen and kidney plus GI, respiratory and cardiovascular systems
Asks about Kehr's sign (left shoulder-tip pain) and screens for anticoagulants
Identifies splenic and renal injury as the leading concerns for LUQ trauma
Interprets dizziness/possible LOC as possible active intra-abdominal bleeding
Gives a sensible differential list (rib fracture/lung contusion, bowel injury, tamponade)
Investigation-led plan: eFAST, CXR, FBE, group and cross-match, urinalysis
IV access, analgesia, IV fluids, admission with close serial monitoring
States stable solid-organ injuries are managed non-operatively; laparotomy reserved for instability/ongoing bleeding
Age-appropriate, reassuring explanation to a frightened adolescent, involving parents/consent

red_flags: Dizziness, possible transient loss of consciousness and worsening LUQ pain after blunt trauma - suspect splenic rupture with active bleeding
Haemodynamic instability (tachycardia, hypotension) mandates immediate resuscitation and surgical involvement
Head strike with loss of consciousness or vomiting triggers a CT-brain pathway and takes priority over the abdomen
Left shoulder-tip pain (Kehr's sign) suggests diaphragmatic irritation from splenic bleeding
australian_guidelines: EMST / ABCDE primary survey is the Australian standard approach to major trauma, with trauma-call activation and history taken in parallel with resuscitation
eFAST (extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) is standard in Australian EDs for blunt chest/abdominal trauma; CT if unstable-then-stabilised or clinical concern persists

Contemporary Australian trauma practice manages haemodynamically stable splenic and renal injuries non-operatively (observation, serial exam, +/- angioembolisation); splenic preservation is prioritised in children to avoid overwhelming post-splenectomy infection - post-splenectomy vaccination (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib) and prophylaxis are mandatory if splenectomy occurs
Standard head-injury triage with GCS/neurological observation charting; call 000 / arrange urgent retrieval to a tertiary trauma centre for significant injury
learning_objectives: Apply a primary-survey framework and structured injury screen to blunt abdominal trauma
Recognise splenic and renal injury as the priority organs in LUQ trauma and elicit Kehr's sign
Use haemodynamic status to drive imaging and the operative-versus-non-operative decision
Adapt communication and consent for an adolescent trauma patient
key_points: Spleen and kidney are the high-risk solid organs in LUQ blunt trauma
eFAST plus CXR, FBE, group and cross-match and urinalysis are the initial investigations
Stable solid-organ injuries are managed non-operatively; instability drives urgent laparotomy
Screen for head injury/LOC first and check for anticoagulants

citations.claim: Screening for loss of consciousness and head strike after a fall with structured monitoring follows standard head-injury triage and neurological observation practice.
citations.source: OXFORD HANDBOOK OF EMERGENCY MEDICINE 5TH EDITION (2020).pdf (p.384)

citations.claim: Conscious state and head injury charting is an AMC-examined competency, supporting asking about head strike and loss of consciousness before focusing on the abdomen.
Urgent plain X-ray as a first-line investigation with early surgical referral in acute emergencies is consistent with the ED management plan of CXR plus early imaging-led surgical decision-making.
